title: Collections
description: Explore C# collection types — List, Dictionary, HashSet, Queue, and Stack — and learn when to use each one.

data.text: Collections are specialized classes for storing and managing groups of related objects. Unlike plain arrays, most collections in C# are dynamic — they grow and shrink automatically as you add or remove items. They live in the System.Collections.Generic namespace and are the backbone of almost every C# application.
Why Use Collections Instead of Arrays?

Arrays have a fixed size set when they are created. If you need more slots later, you must create a brand-new array and copy everything over — a process that is both slow and error-prone. Collections solve this with internal resizing logic that handles growth transparently. They also provide rich methods for searching, sorting, and manipulating data, making your code far more expressive than manual array manipulation.

data.title: Always Prefer Generic Collections
data.text: Always use generic collections (List<T>, Dictionary<TKey, TValue>) from System.Collections.Generic. Non-generic collections like ArrayList and Hashtable require boxing for value types, lose compile-time type safety, and are considered legacy.

List<T> is the most commonly used collection in C#. It stores elements of a single type in a contiguous, zero-indexed sequence. Internally it uses a resizable array — when the array fills up, it allocates a larger one and copies items over, a process that happens infrequently enough to be efficient for most workloads.

data.text: Dictionary<TKey, TValue> stores data as key-value pairs, giving you lightning-fast lookups by key. Under the hood it uses a hash table, which means average-case lookup, insertion, and removal are all O(1). The only constraint is that keys must be unique — adding a duplicate key will throw an exception.

data.text: HashSet<T> is a collection of unique elements with no defined order. It is backed by a hash table just like Dictionary, so Add, Remove, and Contains all run in O(1) on average. Use it when you need to eliminate duplicates or test membership quickly, such as tracking which users have already been processed.

data.content: Removes duplicates and performs fast membership checks

data.text: Queue<T> models a real-world line or waiting list. The first element added (enqueued) is the first one removed (dequeued). It is perfect for task scheduling, breadth-first search algorithms, and any scenario where order of processing must match order of arrival.

data.title: Queue for Task Processing

data.text: Stack<T> models a stack of plates or the browser's back button history. The last element pushed onto the stack is the first one popped off. It is used in undo-redo systems, expression evaluation, depth-first search, and call-stack simulation.

A hash-table-backed collection mapping unique keys to values with O(1) average lookup.

data.title: Exercise: Shopping Cart
data.description: Build a simple shopping cart using the collections you have learned about.
steps: Create a Dictionary<string, int> to map product names to their quantities.
Add at least four products with quantities using the Add method.
Update the quantity of one product using the indexer.
Use ContainsKey to check if a product exists before accessing it.
Use TryGetValue to safely look up a product that does not exist.
Iterate through the dictionary and print each product and its quantity.
Remove one product and print the updated total count.
data.expectedOutcome: A console application that manages products in a cart, safely handles missing keys, and demonstrates the full lifecycle of a Dictionary.

items.question: Can a List<T> hold null values?
items.answer: Yes — if T is a reference type, List<T> can store null entries. If T is a value type (like int), null is not allowed because value types cannot be null by default.

items.question: What happens if I add a duplicate key to a Dictionary?
items.answer: An ArgumentException is thrown at runtime. Use ContainsKey or TryAdd before calling Add if duplicates are possible.

items.question: Is List<T> thread-safe?
items.answer: No. Concurrent reads are fine, but any write operation (Add, Remove, etc.) must be synchronized externally. Use ConcurrentBag<T> or lock statements for multi-threaded scenarios.

items.question: When should I use an array instead of a List<T>?
items.answer: Use an array when the size is truly fixed and known at compile time, or when interoperability with APIs that require arrays is needed. For all other cases, List<T> is preferred.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: List<T> is your go-to for dynamic, ordered collections
Dictionary<TKey, TValue> provides O(1) lookups by key
HashSet<T> guarantees uniqueness with fast Contains checks
Queue<T> is FIFO — first in, first out
Stack<T> is LIFO — last in, first out
Always use generic collections from System.Collections.Generic
Use TryGetValue over indexer access when the key might be missing
data.takeaway: Choosing the right collection makes your code more efficient and easier to read. Start with List<T> and Dictionary when you are unsure.
